rows.description: A teenager follows a trend, a stream of study or a risky challenge because many peers do, and feels anxious about standing out.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult invests, votes for or joins something because it is popular and assumes many people cannot be wrong. Popularity is treated as evidence.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A mature person asks why she wants it and what she would choose if nobody knew, then joins the crowd or leaves it deliberately.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Teacher or elder is always right [Actor]
rows.description: A child accepts anything a teacher or elder says, even when a fact contradicts it, and feels afraid to question. Respect and fear are blended together.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager weighs whether to trust a parent, coach or influencer who sounds sure. Learning that titles do not guarantee truth begins here, awkwardly.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A young trainee follows a senior's unsafe or unethical instruction because refusing feels disrespectful. Culture of hierarchy can make polite objection feel impossible.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A confident professional asks how a claim was reached, offers evidence politely, and separates respect for the person from agreeing with the idea.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A leader notices staff never disagree in meetings and realises his title mutes them. He invites dissent early and thanks people who bring bad news.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: My friends are the good ones [Actor]
rows.description: A child shares more with his own group and says the other class is bad. Even arbitrary teams quickly feel like us and them.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A schoolchild cheers his own house unfairly and excuses its fouls while calling the same acts cheating from others. Belonging feels good and bends fairness.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
